title: Pawns.
reviewNotes: Montage, captions and native complete later diagrams reviewed. Begin before e8=Q at141 seconds in the complete eight-piece later diagram: White Kh1/e7 against Kd3/Bb6/c6/d5/g5/h5. Native33 confirms e7/Bb6 and all four black pawns; native34/35 show Qe8. This version differs from Beautiful Move Alert: its bishop is on b6 rather than b4, and g-pawn on g5 rather than g6. Both are reconstructed and verified separately. Promotion still leaves eight pieces. A complete finite White strategy checks every Black defense through exact supported winning endings; the three guided post-promotion replies are explicitly independent representative continuations. Earlier Nb4 interference and the a-pawn diversion remain outside this selected proof.
transcript: Pawns are a fascinating thing. Each one of them is worth only one point. And yet together, they become an unstoppable force. In this position, it seems like there's no way to make progress. Every single pawn push is stopped by one of the black pawns or one of the black pieces. And we all know that a bishop in an endame is far more valuable than a knight. So, it seems like this game is about to fizzle out to a draw. But white is not a fool and it knows the true power of the pawns. So, white plays H5. Of course, if nothing is done, this pawn is simply going to run and promote. But the pawn can be captured, but white has a plan and it follows up with G6. Same thing. If nothing is done, the pawn is simply going to promote. So, it has to be taken. And now with this little maneuver, white has freed up a path for the E pawn, which gets pushed, but black is not that naive. And of course, it stops the promotion with bishop to A3. and it doesn't seem like there's any progress to be made. The knight cannot help. It's going to take too many moves to defend the E square. And in the meantime, black is simply going to eat all of the remaining pawns. So, it seems like white has actually wasted the lives of two brave warriors for nothing. But that's not the case because white has the stunning and incredible knight to B4, giving up his last piece. But of course, this blocks the view of the bishop. And if the king takes, now the king blocks the view of the bishop and we can simply push the pawn, promoting it to a queen. But wait a second. What if the bishop takes and still guards the pawn? Well, now the a pawn can march up and the bishop is preventing the king from coming to stop it. And bishops are known for being particularly bad at stopping two pawns because now after a move like king takes D3, white can play A5 and sacrifice the pawn. But if the pawn is taken, the bishop is distracted by the E pawn. And with the last pawn, we can get a queen. So black needs to guard both pawns at the same time and play something flexible like bishop to C5. But now the pawn simply keeps going up. And no matter what happens, the pawn is going to reach A7 and the bishop has no choice. It has to stop one of the two pawns and the other one is going to get a new queen.
